tfn.s: In 2006, Karl and another explorer went across the Bering Strait on ice.
tfn.why: The text says: "In 2006, he and another explorer crossed the Bering Strait on moving sea ice."
The text says he reached Dover on that date and still had around 400 kilometres left to walk to Hull.

tfn.s: Karl and the other explorer were arrested when they arrived in Russia.
tfn.why: The text says the authorities arrested them because they had not entered at an official border point.

tfn.s: His son has joined him for part of the walk.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say whether Karl's son has walked with him.

tfn.s: Karl has missed much of his son's childhood.
tfn.why: The text says: "Karl has missed years with his family, including much of his son's childhood."

focus.note: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word. The small word changes the meaning, so learn the two words together.

items.s: We were tired, but we carried ____ walking until dark.
The engine broke ____ in the middle of the desert.
He finally gave ____ smoking after twenty years.
Her grandmother looked ____ her when her parents travelled.
Watch ____ for snakes on the path.
Our guide was ____ about the weather, so we packed only light clothes.
Losing his passport was the biggest ____ to the trip, but he found a way to continue.
After several ____, including a broken ankle, the team still finished the race.

items.s: By the time he reached Dover, he ____ for almost 28 years.

If he had used a vehicle, he ____ his own rules.

tfn.s: According to the text, paperwork delayed Bushby about as much as the wild landscapes did.
tfn.why: The text says paperwork "became as much of an obstacle as the wilderness".

tfn.s: When he landed in Britain, the distance still to walk was much smaller than the distance already behind him.
tfn.why: The text says about 400 kilometres remained, compared with "the thousands of kilometres behind him".

tfn.s: Bushby's original estimate of 12 years was close to the real time.
tfn.why: The text calls the estimate "wildly optimistic" and the walk has taken almost 28 years.

tfn.s: A film company is making a documentary about the expedition.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not mention any documentary about the expedition.

tfn.s: Bushby and Kieffer needed about two days to cross the Bering Strait.
tfn.why: The text says they "spent roughly two weeks crossing the frozen Bering Strait".

focus.note: Many phrasal verbs have more than one meaning, so read the whole sentence before you choose the small word.

items.s: The long walk turned ____ to be harder than the hikers had expected.

match.d: refusing to accept any change or exception
get into trouble with people in authority

items.s: The first border incident ____ years of legal and bureaucratic difficulty.

tfn.s: The writer implies that officials were harder for Bushby to deal with than the terrain.
tfn.why: The text says walking was the straightforward part, while "persuading officials" to let him continue was not.

tfn.s: Bushby swam the Caspian Sea before the pandemic began.
tfn.why: The text mentions the pandemic first and dates the Caspian swim to 2024.

tfn.s: Bushby's son has criticised his father's decision to keep walking.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text only says Bushby has been absent for much of his son's life.

tfn.s: The writer suggests the end of the walk may be harder personally than physically.
tfn.why: The text says the final miles may need less stamina, but the transition to everyday life offers "no marked trail".

tfn.s: The writer presents the expedition as a straightforward success with no real costs.
tfn.why: The text says its human costs "resist such a tidy conclusion".

speak.title: Role-play: a very long trip
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: You want to leave your job and walk across a whole country. You will be away for a year. Explain why it matters to you and answer your friend's worries.

b.text: You are worried about your friend's plan. Ask about money, safety and family. Try to agree on a plan, or a shorter trip.

phrases: I've always wanted to do something like this.
What if you run out of money?
I'd miss my family, but I can't give up now.
Have you thought about the risks?
We could split the trip into two parts.
That's a fair point, I hadn't thought of that.
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: did you agree on a plan, and who gave way?
